title: GLM-5.4: A 750B Model That Runs Its Layers Twice
summary: Z.ai's GLM-5.4 is the first flagship built on a Loop Transformer — 28 of its 78 layers run twice per token, claiming 2T–3T class intelligence from 750B parameters, while shipping with no public benchmarks, no API, and no weights.
content:
On November 23, Z.ai released GLM-5.4, a 750-billion-parameter model with an unusual trick at its core: it runs 28 of its layers twice. The lab, formerly Zhipu AI, calls the design a Loop Transformer, and says it puts the model in the same intelligence class as models with two to three trillion parameters — up to four times its size — for a fraction of the weight memory. The architecture is genuinely interesting. The launch is also unusually thin on proof.

What shipped

GLM-5.4 is built on the GLM-5 base model, not trained from scratch. Z.ai took an already pre-trained network and converted its middle 28 layers into a shared block that executes for two iterations per token, refining the hidden state on the second pass. Total layer passes rise from 78 to 106 — roughly 36% more compute per token — while the parameter count stays put.

That trade is the whole point. Parameters are what you pay for in memory: a 750B model fits on fewer GPUs than a 2T one. Depth of computation is what you pay for in time. Looping buys the second with the first already spent. Z.ai is blunt that looped models trained from scratch underperform normal ones under the same budget, which is why it retrofitted a pre-trained base instead of starting over.

Three engineering changes make the loop deployable. Per-token gates write the first pass's updates into the residual stream cautiously and the second pass's at full strength, which stops activation scales from blowing up across iterations. A hybrid KV cache lets the second pass reuse the first pass's sparse KV selection while keeping its own sliding window, so an extra loop costs one window rather than a full context cache. And the second pass reuses the first pass's sparse attention indices, so indexing adds nothing. Together those keep a one-million-token context affordable.

What the evidence actually shows

Here the launch gets thin. Z.ai published no benchmark table. No API, no weights, no leaderboard entry — GLM-5.4 is live only inside the company's Coding Plan, ZCode, and chat, with an API listed as "coming soon" and open weights promised after "safety hardening."

The numbers that do exist come from an ablation, not the flagship. On a 30B model with the same architecture, a looped and an unlooped version with identical parameter counts were compared: the looped one gained clear ground for about 10% more training compute, with the largest jumps on math, science, and long-context tasks. Output length also fell 10–14% on GPQA-Diamond and MMLU-Pro, meaning part of the reasoning moved off the page and into the extra depth.

That is a real result, measured at a twenty-fifth of the scale. "Comparable to 2T–3T models" is a claim about the 750B model, and nothing public supports it yet.

The weakness Z.ai names itself

GLM-5.4 gets caught in "marathon thinking" loops. Longer reflection does raise accuracy, the company says, but it also means you pay for tokens that circle. At up to 200 tokens per second off-peak, and 70–80 at peak load, raw speed is not the constraint. Verbosity might be.

The demos are more persuasive than the scores: a self-narrated music video, a complete game, an interactive 3D scene built from pure GLSL, and a six-axis robotic arm modeled in FreeCAD to engineering tolerance. That is coding generalized past software, which is the actual thesis of the release.

Takeaway

Looping is the most interesting architectural idea in open models since mixture-of-experts, because it attacks the real bottleneck: intelligence per byte of weight memory. GLM-5.4 is the first flagship to ship it at 750B scale, and the details — the gates, the shared KV cache, the index reuse — are the kind of thing other labs will copy within months.

But a launch without scores is a launch you cannot evaluate. Wait for the benchmark table, the API, and ideally the weights before moving a coding workflow onto it. The architecture deserves to be taken seriously. This particular release is a promise, not a receipt.

Sources: Z.ai, "GLM-5.4: Toward Generalized Coding with Our First Loop Transformer" (Nov 23, 2026); Tech Times, "Z.ai's GLM-5.4 aims to match models up to four times its size by running 28 layers twice" (Nov 2026); i-SCOOP, "GLM-5.4 runs its layers twice to punch above its weight, but ships without scores, an API or weights" (Nov 2026).
